hints: Integrate velocity intervals to get changes in x, then use y(5)=14−x(5) to fix the otherwise unknown origin.
Do not let a negative signed area cancel path length; compare one-sided slopes at the corner.
units.reconstruct: The y reading gives x(5)=14−10=4 m. From 0 to 5 s signed displacement is 3×3−2×2=+5 m, hence x(0)=4−5=−1 m. Then x(3)=−1+9=8 m, x(5)=4 m, x(7)=4+2=6 m. Total displacement=+9−4+2=+7 m, matching 6−(−1)=7 m; distance=9+4+2=15 m. In y=14−x the signed velocities are −3,+2,−1 m/s. At t=3 s, +3 and −2 m/s are the unequal one-sided velocities, so no unique instantaneous velocity follows from an ideal corner. The cart passes x=0 during the first interval at t=1/3 s while moving +3 m/s; position zero does not mean stopped.
units.diagnosis: Distinguish an unfixed position origin, wrong sign on an area, wrong conversion between frames, and treating a corner as a smooth unique velocity. Evaluate each submitted model and number separately.
units.repair: Reconstruct x backwards from the measured y anchor and use a second independent signed area ledger. Explain the origin and corner constraints.
units.boundaryPrompt: Suppose the last velocity step from t=5 to 7 s changes to −2 m/s, with every earlier reading unchanged. Determine the new x(7), the whole-trip displacement and path length.

rubric.expected: Signed-area inverse with a position anchor
rubric.repair: First choose the velocity-area relation and an external position anchor; a graph of velocity has no absolute origin.
The observed y(5)=10 gives x(5)=4, so subtract the first 5 s of signed areas to recover x(0).
Add the last signed area +2 m to the calibrated x(5)=4 m.
Add magnitudes of interval displacements 9+4+2, not their signed sum.
Since y=14−x, the y velocity has the opposite sign to the first x velocity.

rubric.expected: Unequal one-sided velocities; no unique value
rubric.repair: The line approaching the join has +3 m/s; leaving it has −2 m/s. An ideal corner has no single slope.

hints: Name the bumper's repulsive magnitude C, using +C on B and −C on A; treat each accelerometer independently.
Solve 18−C=3×a_A and C−4=2×a_B; then compare the centre-of-mass result with the external force ledger.
units.reconstruct: For A, 18−C=3×2=6 N, hence C=12 N left on A; for B, C−4=2×4=8 N, hence C=12 N right on B. The equations agree, so the action–reaction pair is consistent. The total external force is +18−4=+14 N; the COM acceleration is +14/5=2.8 m/s², also (3×2+2×4)/5=+2.8 m/s². A compressed bumper can be unloading while the carts separate and have distinct accelerations. These readings are not compatible with maintained rigid contact: that constraint would require both to accelerate at +2.8 m/s² and a different contact force. Actual persistence requires relative-motion/compression evidence.
units.diagnosis: Check contact-model selection before the 12 N arithmetic. Confusing rigid and compliant interaction is a model error even if two force equations happen to balance.
units.repair: Label receiving bodies, validate both independent force equations, state the compliant instant and test relative acceleration. Contrast maintained rigid contact using the combined-body constraint.
units.boundaryPrompt: Suppose the bumper is replaced by a rigid, locked connector while both motor and brake forces remain unchanged. Determine the common acceleration and connector force and explain why the original sensor pair cannot persist.

rubric.expected: Compliant unloading bumper; unequal acceleration possible
rubric.repair: First distinguish the compressed bumper's transient mechanics from a rigid kinematic constraint.
Use the B free-body equation C−4=2×4, and verify independently against A:18−C=3×2.
The only horizontal external forces on A+B are +18 and −4 N, divided by the total mass 5 kg.

rubric.expected: Both carts must have equal acceleration
rubric.repair: Rigid maintained contact imposes a_A=a_B. A spring bumper does not.

hints: Conserve energy separately: ΔU=(P_in−P_out)Δt for each system before deciding how the energy is stored.
Only after selecting the phase regime use Δm=ΔU/L or ΔT=ΔU/C. The two formulas do not mean the same thing.
units.reconstruct: For either sample net energy is (90−30)×120=7200 J. A has two phases coexisting at the melting point, so its internal energy goes into melting Δm=7200/180000=0.040 kg, with ΔT=0 K under the stated maintained plateau. B has no transition so ΔT=7200/600=12 K. Both gained 7200 J internal energy; temperature alone did not determine that energy change.
units.diagnosis: First decide whether the measurements support a melting plateau or fixed-phase sensible heating. Check the net power calculation, latent unit conversion and rate-versus-energy distinction before diagnosing arithmetic.
units.repair: Draw system boundaries for A and B; calculate ΔU first, then map the energy to the correct storage state, and falsify the other formula under the stated phase conditions.
units.boundaryPrompt: For the next 120 s, A's heat loss is increased to exactly 90 W while input stays 90 W and its two phases still coexist. What changes in internal energy, melted mass and temperature can be concluded from this constant-rate model?

rubric.expected: A: phase plateau; B: sensible heating
rubric.repair: Use the mixed solid/liquid observation before choosing the energy storage equation.
Subtract loss power from input, then multiply by the 120 s interval.
For the mixed-phase plateau divide net energy by latent heat expressed in J/kg.
Use ΔT=ΔU/C for the unchanged-phase solid B, not sample A.

hints: Convert each emission-referenced time to a whole path length before using any delay.
Squaring the two paths gives (d_s−d_m)² and (d_s+d_m)². The stated order chooses a sign.
units.reconstruct: Direct length L_dir=325×0.040=13 m. Reflected L_ref≈325×0.046154=15.00005 m≈15 m (rounding). From 13²−12²=25, d_s−d_m=+5 m because the source is farther; from 15²−12²=81, d_s+d_m≈9 m. Hence d_s=7 m and d_m=2 m. Verify direct √(12²+5²)=13 m and reflected √(12²+9²)=15 m. Arrival separation≈46.154−40.000=6.154 ms, below 7 ms; the two pulses are unresolved by the specified detector. Without near/far ordering, swapping 7 and 2 gives the same two arrival times.
units.diagnosis: Check whether you treated reflected arrival time as excess delay, chose a plus rather than minus leg for the direct path, or omitted the near/far sign ambiguity. Compare the recovered distances against both original lengths.
units.repair: Reconstruct the two Pythagorean lengths from emission times, solve for sum and signed difference, check the virtual image and threshold.
units.boundaryPrompt: If the same apparatus reveals the microphone is farther from the wall than the source, but both measured path lengths remain 13 m and 15 m, what distances are consistent? Explain the two-arrival ambiguity.

rubric.repair: Both arrival times are since emission. Construct the direct and mirrored-reflection path separately.
Find the sum of wall distances from the reflected path and the signed difference from the direct path.
The source is stated farther from the wall, fixing the sign of d_s−d_m.
Subtract two emission-referenced times; do not halve a difference of arrival times.
Compare the two arrival separation against the detector threshold, not the total reflected travel time.
